news.title: Trump Says Iran War 'Won't Go Much Longer'; Hints At Endgame As Tehran Pushes Hormuz Deal
news.text: US President Donald Trump has indicated that the prolonged conflict with Iran could be approaching its conclusion, saying he believes the war "will end pretty soon" as diplomatic efforts surrounding the Strait of Hormuz appear to gather momentum. Trump's remarks come as Iran confirmed that discussions with Oman over a new shipping arrangement in the strategically vital waterway have entered the final drafting stage, raising hopes of a possible de-escalation after months of military confrontation. Speaking to reporters, Trump expressed confidence that Tehran's ability to sustain the conflict was diminishing. "I started the very important excursion into the Islamic Republic of Iran; it was a very important excursion because they can't have a nuclear weapon... I think the war is going to end soon, I don't think they can go much longer," Trump said. The President also acknowledged that the conflict had placed pressure on parts of America's weapons inventory, although he insisted the United States remained well-equipped. "We have certain types of munitions that are very powerful, that we have virtually unlimited supply. We have others where it's a little bit tighter," Trump said. He added that US defence manufacturers were expanding production capacity, including new facilities for Patriot air defence interceptors and Tomahawk cruise missiles, as Washington works to replenish stocks following months of sustained military operations. Hormuz Talks Move Towards Final Draft Trump's comments coincided with fresh signals from Tehran that negotiations over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz are nearing completion. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran and Oman had reached the final drafting stage of an agreement covering the geographical coordinates of a new shipping route through the strait. According to Baghaei, a joint statement would be issued "if certain parties do not obstruct this process," in an apparent reference to the United States. Iran has maintained that any understanding with Oman would not restore shipping conditions to their pre-war status, arguing that the disruption resulted from the US naval blockade imposed on Iranian ports during the conflict. Officials in Tehran have also suggested that any broader agreement remains linked to the lifting of restrictions on Iranian maritime trade. Washington Also Signals Diplomatic Progress Washington has similarly indicated that negotiations remain active. Earlier, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said discussions with Tehran had made meaningful progress. "We are in talks with the Iranians, and I think there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the Strait and move towards a more normalised position in this conflict," Bessent told CNBC. He added that any agreement should guarantee "freedom of movement" through one of the world's most strategically important maritime chokepoints. When asked separately about the Strait of Hormuz, Trump suggested commercial navigation had not completely ceased. "It has been sort of open right now," the President said. Major Issues Still Unresolved Despite the increasingly optimistic rhetoric from both Washington and Tehran, several fundamental disagreements remain unresolved. Iran continues to insist that any future navigation arrangement reflects its security concerns and sovereignty claims, while US officials have repeatedly maintained that international shipping must remain free from Iranian control, permits or transit fees. The conflicting positions suggest that although negotiations appear to be advancing, the broader political and military dispute underpinning the five-month conflict has yet to be fully resolved. For now, Trump's prediction that the war may end "pretty soon" reflects growing diplomatic momentum, but whether that optimism translates into a durable settlement will likely depend on resolving the outstanding disputes surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and the wider US-Iran confrontation.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump has expressed optimism that the months-long conflict with Iran could end "pretty soon", even as Tehran says it is in the final stages of drafting a Strait of Hormuz agreement with Oman.
news.author: Yuvraj Tyagi

news.title: Arson Suspect Timed Spokane, Washington, Fire for High Wind Day
news.text: (Bloomberg) -- The 37-year old man suspected of starting one of the fires burning around Spokane, Washington told a detective that he planned the arson attack for Sunday to coincide with a “high winds” day, according to court documents.That blaze was one of three that destroyed roughly 700 buildings and forced 70,000 people to evacuate earlier this week. Aaron Farinacci, of Spokane, was arrested Monday. Police said he admitted to starting other fires in the area since last year, according to court documents. Detective Michael Drapeau said Farinacci waived his constitutional rights and decided to answer police questions.Sunday’s blaze was one of 16 other large fires burning this week in Washington state. The smoke has clouded skies above Seattle and Portland, Oregon, prompting air quality warnings. Fire risks are set to intensify in coming days. Red-flag fire warnings have been posted across parts of Oregon and Washington, including Spokane, where a dry weather front is expected to bring wind gusts up to 30 miles (48 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Weather Service.Conditions across the region and neighboring states caused the US Storm Prediction Center to forecast an elevated risk, or level one of three, for Friday. “A combination of strong winds, low relative humidity and warm temperatures can contribute to extreme fire behavior,” the weather service said in the warning that expires at 11 p.m. on Saturday. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson, who frequently challenged President Donald Trump in court as the state’s attorney general during his first term, invited the president to visit Spokane and see the wildfire devastation firsthand in a post on X.Firefighters have built containment lines around three fires that have burned more than 10,000 acres near Spokane, allowing some residents to return home, Washington Commissioner of Public Lands Dave Upthegrove said Wednesday in a Facebook post. Even so, 16 large fires remain active statewide, according to the Washington Department of Natural Resources.Meanwhile, The US Postal Service warned that wildfires in Washington and Oregon could delay mail and package deliveries.Little relief is expected from the weather. Air quality alerts remain in effect across much of the Pacific Northwest and neighboring Idaho as wildfire smoke blankets the region. That has pushed air quality into dangerous and very dangerous categories in some areas, including parts of southern Canada.There is no rain in the forecast across the region and with an El Niño strengthening in the Pacific, the region may see dry weather in the long term, said David Roth, a senior branch forecaster at the US Weather Prediction Center. Through Aug. 4, more than 93% of Washington’s lands were abnormally dry and almost 64% were in drought, according to the US Drought Monitor. Oregon was almost 91% in drought. El Niños tend to suppress the jet stream across the US, which means most storms pass south of Washington and Oregon, Roth said. Currently the US Climate Prediction Center calls for a slight chance of above normal rainfall in eastern Washington and Oregon from Aug. 13 to 19 and near average elsewhere.More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

news.title: Sen. Marsha Blackburn wins GOP nomination for Tennessee governor
news.text:
In deep-red Tennessee, which has not elected a Democratic governor in over a decade or senator since 1990, Blackburn is largely expected to coast through the general election and keep the governor’s mansion in Republican hands.

Blackburn and Rose each vied for the GOP gubernatorial bid by pledging their allegiance to President Donald Trump‘s agenda, who withheld an endorsement in the three-way race. Each of their campaign websites and video advertisements features imagery of the president, as they focused on economic issues and backing Trump’s stances on immigration and election integrity.

news.title: White House’s push to delay hemp product ban could have big benefit to Susie Wiles’ son-in-law: reports
news.text:
The Trump administration’s push to delay a ban on intoxicating hemp products could have a big benefit to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles’ son-in-law, according to new reports. 

Last fall, President Donald Trump signed a spending bill to end the longest shutdown in history, which included a ban on hemp products containing certain amounts of THC, the main intoxicating compound found in cannabis. Now, the White House seems to have reversed course, reportedly pushing lawmakers on Capitol Hill to delay the very ban Trump enacted. 

While the White House maintains that its new stance on the issue is in the interest of the American people, reports from The New York Times and MS NOW suggest that the move would allegedly benefit Wiles’ son-in-law, Bret Worley.

Worley, who married Wiles’ younger daughter Caroline in June, is the CEO of MC Nutraceuticals, a global supplier of hemp products. His company has been reportedly pushing industry allies to pressure lawmakers to delay the ban on hemp products, which is set to take effect on November 12. 

In a new stopgap spending measure to avoid another shutdown at the end of September, senators added a provision delaying the implementation of the hemp product ban to December 11, reports say. The measure will be up for a vote this week. 

“The Chief of Staff has never lobbied in favor of this or any other position on hemp with Capitol Hill,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement to the media.

“The only interest guiding the Trump administration’s decision-making is the best interest of the American people, and the Administration continues to explore a Gold Science Standard-based framework on hemp to expand treatment options for American veterans and patients,” Desai said.

The Independent has reached out to the White House and Worley for comment. 

As the spending measure was announced Sunday, MC Nutraceuticals said in an email to prospective buyers that the hemp industry now had “a seat at the table,” according to the Times. 

Senator Ted Budd, a North Carolina Republican, has pushed against the delay of the hemp product ban, writing on X Monday, “I'm offering an amendment to the CR [continuing resolution] to strip out an extension of the hemp loophole to ensure unregulated, dangerous intoxicants are not sold, especially to kids.”

The Food and Drug Administration wrote in an October 2024 notice that it was concerned about products containing delta-8 THC “in forms such as candy, chips, cereals and other foods that appeal to children.”

Budd told MS NOW that the White House’s new stance on the ban is “absolutely ridiculous.”

“We fixed this thing last year. We fixed it last November. They’ve had nine months to work on this, so why, all of a sudden, pop up for some seemingly innocent delay?” he said.

But Senator Shelley Moore Capito, a West Virginia Republican, said the delay was worth it if it meant avoiding another shutdown. Last fall’s shutdown caused major airport disruptions due to staff shortages as agencies lacked the funds to pay government workers. 

“I prefer that we don’t extend it, but I can live with a monthlong extension in exchange for keeping the government open,” Capito told the Times.
news.summary: Bret Worley, who married Wiles’ younger daughter Caroline in June, is the CEO of a global hemp product supplier

news.title: US President Donald Trump signs orders to limit US birthright citizenship
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has signed two executive orders in another attempt to curtail birthright citizenship.

The narrowed attempt is his second crack at challenging the provision of the US Constitution and comes after the Supreme Court rejected his previous effort.

Limiting birthright citizenship has been one of the top priorities in Trump’s crackdown on immigration, with the White House taking particular aim at what it calls “birth tourism” — in which pregnant foreigners travel to the US to give birth.

Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today Arrow

After his June 30 setback in the Supreme Court, Trump called on Congress to act but on Thursday he opted for executive orders, which set policy but are not legally binding.

The court said Trump’s earlier effort to restrict birthright citizenship was unconstitutional.

The administration argues the new directive does not fall within the limits of the Supreme Court ruling, allowing it to expand who would be considered ineligible for birthright citizenship, including those who would arrive for “birth tourism” purposes.

The categories, Trump’s order said, “do not fall within the rule of birthright citizenship as announced by the Supreme Court”.

“That practice of birth tourism is, as of the signing of this order, hereby banned,” White House aide Stephen Miller said at the signing ceremony in the Oval Office.

“What that means is that no one in the world is anymore allowed to obtain a visa for this fraudulent purpose.”

‘It’s a disgrace’

The Centre for Immigration Studies, which supports lower levels of immigration, estimated in an analysis in 2020 that between 20,000 to 25,000 mothers came to the US for birth tourism in a year-long period between 2016 and 2017.

There were 3.6 million births in the US in 2025.

The executive orders also limit the rights of children born to foreign government employees in the US and children of people who are classified as alien enemies.

The orders could also affect people born in US territories, should Congress enact a proposed law to end automatic citizenship there.

Trump’s new orders are likely to be challenged in court.

“We had a very unfortunate decision in the Supreme Court concerning birthright. It was close, but a very, very unfortunate decision,” Trump said of the 6-3 vote.

“People are building businesses around it. That’s not the way it’s supposed to work. It’s a disgrace.”

There are no official figures tallying the number of foreigners who come to the US for the explicit purpose of giving birth and obtaining citizenship for their children, or the cost to taxpayers.

No US law outright bars birth tourism but a federal regulation implemented in 2020 during Trump’s first term prohibits using temporary tourist and business visas for the primary purpose of obtaining US citizenship for a newborn.

People who engage in birth tourism schemes could be prosecuted for fraud or other related crimes.
news.author: Kristina Cooke
